Doctors have absolute discretion to conceal risks under therapeutic privilege
Patients are presumed to know all surgical risks under the doctrine of volenti
A doctor has a duty to take reasonable care to ensure a patient is aware of any material risks involved in recommended treatment (moving away from Bolam)
9.explanation: Montgomery shifted from doctor-focused Bolam to patient-focused autonomy: doctors must advise of any material risk to which a reasonable patient would attach significance.

9.question: In Nettleship v Weston (1971), what standard of care is expected of a learner driver?
options: The standard of a reasonably competent, qualified driver; inexperience is no defence
A reduced standard reflecting their beginner status and learner plates
No standard of care applies until they pass their practical driving examination
The standard of an ordinary reasonable passenger
9.explanation: In Nettleship v Weston, Lord Denning held that a learner driver must meet the objective standard of an ordinary, reasonably competent and experienced driver.

9.question: In Mullin v Richards (1998), how is the standard of care assessed for a child defendant?
options: The standard of an ordinary reasonable parent
Children under 16 cannot be sued in tort under any circumstances
The standard of an ordinarily prudent and reasonable child of the defendant's exact age
The standard of an adult teacher supervising the classroom
9.explanation: In Mullin v Richards (ruler fight at school), a child's standard of care is that of an ordinary, reasonable child of the same age.

9.question: What is the doctrine of 'res ipsa loquitur' (the thing speaks for itself) in negligence (Scott v London & St Katherine Docks Co 1865)?
options: A rule of evidence where the accident's nature permits an inference of negligence because the thing was under D's exclusive control and wouldn't happen without negligence
A principle barring claims where the defendant is an unincorporated club
A statutory defence exempting public dock authorities from liability
A rule requiring claimants to produce three eyewitnesses in every tort trial
9.explanation: Res ipsa loquitur applies when the thing causing damage was under D's exclusive control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence.

9.question: What test is used to determine 'factual causation' in the tort of negligence?
options: The Reasonable Foreseeability test
The 'But For' test (Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital Management Committee 1969)
The Remoteness test
The Caparo three-stage test
9.explanation: Factual causation is established by the 'but for' test: C must prove on balance of probabilities that 'but for' D's breach, the damage would not have occurred.

9.question: In Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital (1969), why did the doctor's negligent failure to examine the patient NOT cause his death?
options: Because the patient had refused to pay the prescription fee
Because hospitals had crown immunity in 1969
Because the patient had consumed lethal arsenic and would have died anyway, even if the doctor had examined and treated him immediately
Because the doctor was off duty and volunteering his time
9.explanation: In Barnett, the doctor was in breach, but factual causation failed under the 'but for' test: the patient would have died from arsenic poisoning regardless of treatment.

9.question: In Wilsher v Essex Area Health Authority (1988), why did the medical negligence claim fail where there were five distinct possible causes of blindness?
options: Because junior doctors are judged by lower professional standards
Because the hospital had exceeded its annual negligence insurance budget
Because premature infants cannot bring civil claims in tort
Because the claimant could not prove on balance of probabilities that the negligent administration of excess oxygen caused the blindness rather than natural causes
9.explanation: In Wilsher, there were five separate possible causes; C could not prove that D's breach caused or materially contributed to the injury on balance of probabilities.

9.question: In Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd (2002), how did the House of Lords resolve causation where a worker inhaled asbestos across multiple employers?
options: The claim was dismissed entirely because the worker could not identify the single fatal fibre
Each employer who materially increased the risk of developing mesothelioma was held jointly and severally liable
The manufacturer of the protective masks was held strictly liable
Liability was allocated randomly by a court lottery
9.explanation: In Fairchild, the House of Lords applied a modified approach: each employer who materially increased the risk of mesothelioma was liable.

9.question: What is a 'novus actus interveniens' in negligence?
options: A new intervening act that breaks the chain of legal causation between defendant's breach and claimant's ultimate damage
A formal written retraction of a defamatory allegation
An agreement to submit a personal injury claim to binding arbitration
A preliminary injunction issued by the High Court Chancery Division
9.explanation: A novus actus interveniens is an intervening act (by a third party, claimant, or natural event) so independent and unreasonable that it breaks causation.

9.question: In McKew v Holland & Hannen & Cubitts (1969), why did the claimant's own action break the chain of causation?
options: Because the employer had offered to provide a motorized wheelchair
Because the claimant had signed a full discharge of liability
Because walking down stairs is an illegal trespass in public buildings
Attempting to descend a steep flight of stairs without a handrail or assistance with an injured leg was an entirely unreasonable act
9.explanation: In McKew, C's conduct in descending stairs without aid despite his weak leg was so unreasonable that it was a novus actus interveniens breaking causation.

9.question: What landmark case established the modern test for 'remoteness of damage' in negligence, replacing the direct consequences test of Re Polemis?
options: Rylands v Fletcher (1868)
Donoghue v Stevenson (1932)
Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Morts Dock & Engineering Co (The Wagon Mound No 1) (1961)
Hadley v Baxendale (1854)
9.explanation: The Wagon Mound (No 1) established that damage is too remote unless it was of a kind or type that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the breach.

9.question: In Hughes v Lord Advocate (1963), why was the burn injury NOT too remote even though the paraffin lamp exploded in an unforeseeable manner?
options: Because the type of injury (burns from fire) was reasonably foreseeable; the precise sequence of events or exact manner of harm does not need to be foreseeable
Because the post office workers had abandoned the manhole
Because children playing on roads are protected by strict liability statutes
Because paraffin is an explosive substance under petroleum legislation
9.explanation: In Hughes v Lord Advocate, burn injury was foreseeable; the defendant is liable even if the injury occurs through an unexpected or unforeseeable mechanism.

9.question: What is the 'Eggshell Skull Rule' (Smith v Leech Brain & Co Ltd 1962)?
options: A claimant with a pre-existing medical condition is barred from recovering damages
You must take your victim as you find them; if the kind of injury is foreseeable, D is liable for the full extent of harm caused by C's pre-existing vulnerability
Employers must provide carbon-fibre helmets to all factory employees
Compensation is capped at £10,000 for any head or brain injury
9.explanation: Under Smith v Leech Brain, the tortfeasor takes the victim as found; if physical burn was foreseeable, D is liable for cancer triggered by pre-existing condition.

9.question: What statute governs the partial defence of Contributory Negligence in English law?
options: Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945
Crown Proceedings Act 1947
Compensation Act 2006
Civil Liability Act 2018
9.explanation: The Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 provides that damages are reduced proportionally where C's own negligence contributed to the damage.

9.question: What is the legal effect of successfully proving contributory negligence?
options: It is a partial defence that reduces the claimant's damages to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to C's share of responsibility
It transfers the liability to the claimant's motor insurer
It completely dismisses the claim, leaving the claimant with zero damages
It imposes a mandatory criminal fine on the claimant
9.explanation: Contributory negligence is not a complete defence; under the 1945 Act, damages are reduced proportionally according to fault.

9.question: In Froom v Butcher (1976), what standard reduction in damages did Lord Denning suggest for failing to wear a seatbelt?
options: No reduction, as seatbelts were optional in 1976
100% complete dismissal of the personal injury claim
25% reduction if the failure made all the difference to the injuries, and 15% if it would have made the injuries less severe
50% reduction in all motor accident personal injury claims
9.explanation: In Froom v Butcher, Lord Denning set guidelines: 25% reduction if seatbelt would have prevented injury entirely; 15% if it would have reduced injury severity.

9.question: In Sayers v Harlow Urban District Council (1958), why were the claimant's damages reduced by 25% after she was trapped in a public toilet?
options: Because she entered the cubicle without a valid entry ticket
Because public councils enjoyed sovereign immunity from toilet maintenance
Because she failed to shout for help before attempting escape
Because standing on a rotating toilet roll holder to climb out was contributory negligence
9.explanation: In Sayers v Harlow, D was negligent for the defective lock, but C's reliance on a wobbly toilet roll holder was careless, reducing damages by 25%.

9.question: What are the two essential requirements for the complete defence of 'Volenti non fit injuria' (consent / voluntary assumption of risk)?
options: The claimant signed a written waiver in front of a police officer
The activity was classified as an extreme sport under municipal by-laws
The claimant paid a safety deposit before embarking on the activity
The claimant had full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk, AND freely and voluntarily agreed to incur that risk
9.explanation: Volenti requires proof that C had full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk (scienti) and voluntarily accepted the risk of injury (volenti).

9.question: In Morris v Murray (1991), why did the defence of volenti succeed against a passenger who accepted a flight with a heavily drunken pilot?
options: Because the plane crashed on private farmland
Because light aircraft passengers are required by statute to hold pilot licences
Because the flight took place outside civil aviation air corridors
Because getting into a light aircraft with a pilot who had consumed 17 whiskies was so wildly irresponsible as to amount to voluntary assumption of risk
9.explanation: In Morris v Murray, accepting a flight with a drastically drunken pilot was embarking on an enterprise so hazardous that C clearly consented to the risk.

9.question: Under Section 149 of the Road Traffic Act 1988, can a motor vehicle driver rely on the defence of volenti against a passenger?
options: No, unless the vehicle was a heavy goods lorry
Yes, if the journey took place on a private toll road
Yes, provided the passenger knew the driver was unlicensed
No, any agreement between a passenger and driver purporting to negate or restrict liability is of no effect
9.explanation: Section 149 Road Traffic Act 1988 bars the defence of volenti against passengers in motor vehicles on roads.

9.question: In ICI v Shatwell (1965), why did the defence of volenti succeed where two shot-firers disregarded statutory safety regulations?
options: Because trade union agreements supersedes common law tort rules
Because they acted in deliberate, joint defiance of statutory safety rules and employer orders with full knowledge of the catastrophic explosion risk
Because quarry owners are immune from safety regulations
Because the explosives were manufactured overseas
9.explanation: In ICI v Shatwell, the brothers freely and deliberately decided to test detonators in breach of regulations; volenti applied.

9.question: Why does the defence of volenti generally NOT succeed against rescuers (Haynes v Harwood 1935; Baker v T E Hopkins 1959)?
options: Because rescuers are automatically protected by the Emergency Workers Act
Because rescuers act under a moral and social compulsion to save endangered lives, so their actions are not truly voluntary
Because defendants owe a strict absolute duty to all emergency medics
Because rescuers are classified as employees of the emergency services
9.explanation: Rescuers are not volens: the law will not penalise a rescuer acting under a moral urge/duty created by the defendant's wrongdoing.

9.question: What is the common law defence of 'Illegality' (ex turpi causa non oritur actio)?
options: A defence available only to crown prosecutors
A defendant can escape liability by committing a minor summary offense
All contracts involving foreign companies are void for illegality
A claimant cannot base a legal claim upon their own illegal, criminal, or immoral conduct
9.explanation: The illegality defence (ex turpi causa) prevents a claimant from pursuing a claim founded on their own criminal or illegal enterprise.

9.question: In Patel v Mirza (2016), what flexible modern test did the Supreme Court establish for the defence of illegality?
options: An automatic, rigid rule barring any claimant who has ever been convicted of a crime
A requirement that the claimant pay a 50% restitution fee to HM Treasury
Consider the underlying purpose of the prohibition, public policies affected, and whether denying the claim would be a proportionate response
Referral of all illegality questions to the European Court of Human Rights
9.explanation: In Patel v Mirza, Lord Toulson established a policy-based approach: (a) underlying purpose, (b) other public policies, (c) proportionality to avoid incoherence.

9.question: Under what circumstances does the defence of 'Act of God' (vis major) apply in tort (Nichols v Marsland 1876)?
options: Whenever an employee suffers a heart attack while working
Where an extraordinary natural disaster occurs which no human foresight could reasonably anticipate or guard against
Whenever heavy rain occurs during a British autumn
When an industrial strike closes down public utilities
9.explanation: Act of God is an event involving natural causes, without human intervention, so catastrophic that no human foresight could guard against it.

9.question: What does the 'inevitable accident' defence mean in tort?
options: A mechanical defect that is covered by a manufacturer warranty
An collision occurring on a motorway in heavy fog
An accident that occurs at an industrial construction site
An accident which could not have been avoided by the greatest care and skill on the part of the defendant
9.explanation: Inevitable accident applies where an event happens which the defendant could not possibly have prevented by the exercise of reasonable care.

9.question: Under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1934, what happens to a tort cause of action when a party dies?
options: The claim is transferred to the local municipal council
The tort claim is immediately extinguished upon death
The cause of action survives against, or for the benefit of, the deceased person's estate
The claim can only be continued if approved by the Attorney-General
9.explanation: Under the 1934 Act, existing causes of action in tort survive the death of either party for the benefit of or against the estate.

9.question: Under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976, who can bring a claim for loss of dependency following a person's wrongful death?
options: All creditors holding outstanding invoices against the deceased
Specified statutory dependants (e.g., spouse, civil partner, children, cohabitants of 2+ years) who suffered financial dependency on the deceased
Any friend or acquaintance who attended the deceased person's funeral
The deceased's employer seeking compensation for loss of key staff
9.explanation: The Fatal Accidents Act 1976 allows statutory dependants who suffered financial dependency to claim for the loss of that dependency.

9.question: What is 'bereavement damages' under Section 1A of the Fatal Accidents Act 1976?
options: A fixed statutory sum awarded to a spouse, civil partner, cohabitant of 2+ years, or parents of an unmarried minor child
A pension paid monthly by the Department for Work and Pensions
A grant paid by the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority
An unlimited discretionary sum calculated based on the emotional grief of all relatives
9.explanation: Bereavement damages under s.1A FAA 1976 is a fixed statutory lump sum payable to specified close relations (spouse, civil partner, cohabitant, or parents of minor).

9.question: Under the Limitation Act 1980, what is the primary limitation period for bringing an ordinary personal injury negligence claim?
options: Ten years from the date the defendant purchased indemnity insurance
Three years from the date the cause of action accrued or date of knowledge of injury
Six years from the date of the breach of duty
Twelve months from the date of first medical treatment
9.explanation: Under s.11 Limitation Act 1980, personal injury claims have a limitation period of 3 years from the date of accrual or date of knowledge.

9.question: Under the Limitation Act 1980, what is the limitation period for bringing a claim for breach of contract or simple tort (damage to property)?
options: Ten years from the date of initial commercial delivery
Twelve years from the date of the first formal solicitor letter
Three years from the date of the contract breach
Six years from the date the cause of action accrued
9.explanation: Under ss. 2 and 5 Limitation Act 1980, actions founded on tort (other than personal injury) or simple contract must be brought within 6 years.

9.question: What power does the court have under Section 33 of the Limitation Act 1980 in personal injury cases?
options: Power to sentence the defendant to a term of imprisonment
Power to transfer the case to the European Court of Justice
Discretionary power to override the 3-year limitation period if it is equitable to do so having regard to prejudice to both parties
Power to double the damages awarded to the injured claimant
9.explanation: Section 33 gives the court discretionary power to disapply the 3-year time limit for personal injury if equitable, balancing prejudice to both parties.

9.question: In pure negligence, does an action lie without proof of actual damage (actionable per se)?
options: No, unless the breach occurred on a public railway station
No, damage is the gist of negligence; actual damage (physical injury, property damage, or recognized financial harm) must be proven
Yes, negligence is actionable per se without any proof of damage
Yes, provided the defendant acted with gross recklessness
9.explanation: Unlike trespass, negligence is NOT actionable per se; damage is the gist of the action, and C must prove actual recognized damage.

10.question: What statute governs the duty owed by an occupier of premises to lawful visitors in English law?
options: Occupiers' Liability Act 1984
Occupiers' Liability Act 1957
Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Defective Premises Act 1972
10.explanation: The Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 regulates the duty of care that an occupier owes to all lawful visitors to their premises.

10.question: Who is an 'occupier' under the Occupiers' Liability Acts (Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd 1966)?
options: The municipal local council for the geographic district
Anyone who has a sufficient degree of control over premises; there can be more than one occupier simultaneously
Only the registered freehold owner holding legal deeds
The tenant holding the longest leasehold interest
10.explanation: In Wheat v E Lacon, an occupier is anyone with occupational control; both brewery and pub managers were held to be occupiers.

10.question: What is the 'common duty of care' owed to lawful visitors under Section 2(2) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957?
options: A strict duty to guarantee the premises are free of all conceivable hazards
A duty to rebuild any structure older than fifty years
A duty to provide personal security guards for each customer
A duty to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes permitted
10.explanation: S.2(2) OLA 1957 defines the common duty of care: take reasonable care to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using premises for permitted purposes.

10.question: Under Section 2(3)(a) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, what special standard of care is owed to child visitors?
options: Occupiers must ban children from all retail and industrial premises
Children are owed the exact same standard of care as adult visitors
An occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults; premises must be reasonably safe for a child of that age
Occupiers have no duty to children unless accompanied by two adults
10.explanation: S.2(3)(a) provides that an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults, taking into account alluring hazards (Glasgow Corp v Taylor).

10.question: In Phipps v Rochester Corporation (1955), why was the council NOT liable when a five-year-old child fell into an open trench on a housing estate?
options: Because occupiers are entitled to assume that young children will be accompanied and supervised by their parents in places of obvious danger
Because council housing estates are exempt from occupiers' liability
Because the child was trespassing without permission
Because the trench was covered by an Act of God
10.explanation: In Phipps v Rochester, Devlin J held that occupiers can expect prudent parents will not allow unaccompanied young children to wander into danger.

10.question: Under Section 2(3)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, what can an occupier expect regarding skilled persons carrying out their trade (Roles v Nathan 1963)?
options: The specialist is owed a higher duty of care than a domestic visitor
The occupier is strictly liable if the specialist is injured
The occupier must teach the specialist how to operate their own equipment
An occupier may expect that a specialist will appreciate and guard against any special risks ordinarily incident to their calling
10.explanation: In Roles v Nathan (chimney sweeps overcome by carbon monoxide), an occupier can expect specialists to guard against risks incident to their trade.

10.question: Under Section 2(4)(b) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, when is an occupier NOT liable for faulty work done by an independent contractor (Haseldine v Daw 1941)?
options: If it was reasonable to entrust the work to a contractor, the occupier checked contractor competence, and verified the work if reasonably possible
If the contractor was paid in cash without an invoice
Occupiers are always vicariously liable for all contractor errors
If the premises were insured with a registered UK underwriter
10.explanation: S.2(4)(b) protects an occupier for contractor fault if: (1) reasonable to hire contractor; (2) reasonable steps taken to check competence; (3) reasonable checks on work.

10.question: What statute governs the duty owed by occupiers to non-visitors (trespassers) in English law?
options: Occupiers' Liability Act 1957
Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000
Occupiers' Liability Act 1984
Criminal Justice Act 1988
10.explanation: The Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 introduced a limited statutory duty of care towards persons other than visitors (trespassers).

10.question: Which landmark House of Lords case led to the enactment of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 by recognizing a duty of 'common humanity' to child trespassers?
options: British Railways Board v Herrington (1972)
Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council (2004)
Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd (1966)
Donoghue v Stevenson (1932)
10.explanation: In Herrington, the House of Lords established a duty of 'common humanity' to trespassers (child electrified on railway line), prompting the 1984 Act.

10.question: Under Section 1(3) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, what three conditions must be satisfied before a duty arises towards a trespasser?
options: Trespasser was under 18; property was commercial; and warning signs were damaged
Occupier knows/has grounds to know of danger; knows/has grounds to know trespasser is in vicinity; and risk is one against which occupier may reasonably be expected to offer protection
Occupier possessed malice; property was rural; and trespasser was sober
Trespasser suffered financial loss; police were called; and damage was over £1,000
10.explanation: Under s.1(3) OLA 1984, duty arises only if occupier knows/has grounds to know of hazard, knows/suspects trespasser vicinity, and risk reasonably requires protection.

10.question: In Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council (2004), why was the council NOT liable when an adult trespasser dived into a shallow lake and broke his neck?
options: Because swimming is an actionable criminal trespass per se
Because public parks are exempt from occupiers' liability legislation
Because lakes are not classified as 'premises' under the 1984 Act
The danger arose from the claimant's own foolhardy diving, not from the state of the premises, and council had posted clear warning signs
10.explanation: In Tomlinson, the risk arose from C's voluntary dive, not the condition of the lake; the council was not required to spend money preventing adults taking obvious risks.

10.question: Under Section 1(8) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, what type of damage can a trespasser NOT recover?
options: Personal injury
Fatal accident dependency
Psychiatric harm
Damage to property
10.explanation: Section 1(8) of the 1984 Act explicitly excludes liability for damage to property; a trespasser can recover only for death or personal injury.

10.question: What is 'Private Nuisance' in English law?
options: An unlawful and substantial interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or some right over, or in connection with it
A breach of contract regarding the sale of residential real estate
A dispute over commercial trademark infringement
Any physical injury suffered by an individual on a public highway
10.explanation: Private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a person's use, enjoyment, or rights over land (Hunter v Canary Wharf).

10.question: In Hunter v Canary Wharf Ltd (1997), who has standing (locus standi) to sue in private nuisance?
options: Any member of the local public who experienced dust or poor television reception
Only persons with a proprietary interest or right of exclusive possession in the affected land (owner-occupier or tenant with lease)
Anyone living in the property, including children, lodgers, and visitors
Local municipal councillors representing the affected ward
10.explanation: In Hunter v Canary Wharf, the House of Lords ruled that only persons with a proprietary interest in the land (owners, tenants) can sue in private nuisance.

10.question: In Sturges v Bridgman (1879), how did Thesiger LJ illustrate the importance of 'locality' in private nuisance?
options: 'No man may divert a subterranean stream to his neighbor's detriment'
'What would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey'
'The law does not concern itself with trifles'
'An Englishman's home is his sovereign castle'
10.explanation: In Sturges v Bridgman, Thesiger LJ famously observed that character of the neighborhood is relevant: 'what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey'.

10.question: In Robinson v Kilvert (1889), why did the paper manufacturer fail in private nuisance when hot air from the cellar damaged his exceptionally sensitive brown paper?
options: Because manufacturing paper is an illegal trade under common law
Because heating pipes are protected by statutory building codes
Because the tenant had failed to pay the quarterly heating surcharge
A defendant is not liable for damage caused to an abnormally sensitive claimant or use of land if it would not affect an ordinary person or ordinary trade
10.explanation: In Robinson v Kilvert, the heat would not have harmed ordinary paper; the law will not protect abnormally sensitive trade/property in nuisance.

10.question: In Christie v Davey (1893) and Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett (1936), what effect does 'malice' have on an interference that might otherwise be lawful?
options: Malice converts a civil tort into high treason
Malice has no legal relevance to nuisance
Malice doubles the limitation period to twelve years
Malice makes an interference unreasonable and turns it into an actionable nuisance
10.explanation: In Christie v Davey (banging on walls) and Hollywood Silver Fox Farm (firing guns near foxes), deliberate malice rendered the defendant's conduct an actionable nuisance.

10.question: In private nuisance, is 'coming to the nuisance' (claimant moving to the nuisance) a valid defence (Bliss v Hall 1838; Sturges v Bridgman 1879)?
options: No, it is no defence that the claimant came to the nuisance or that the activity was already operating before C arrived
No, unless the claimant purchased the land at a 50% discount
Yes, moving next to an existing business bars any nuisance claim
Yes, provided the business operated for more than twelve months
10.explanation: In Sturges v Bridgman, the physician built his consulting room next to a confectioner's mortar; moving to the nuisance is NO defence.

10.question: What is the defence of 'Prescription' in private nuisance (Sturges v Bridgman 1879)?
options: If the defendant holds an operating permit issued by the municipal council
If the nuisance has continued openly and without interruption as an actionable nuisance against the claimant for at least 20 years, D acquires a prescriptive right
If the claimant fails to complain within 30 days of moving in
If the business was established before the coronation of Queen Victoria
10.explanation: Prescription allows a right to commit private nuisance if it has run openly and continuously as an actionable nuisance for at least 20 years.

10.question: What is 'Public Nuisance' in English law (Attorney-General v PYA Quarries Ltd 1957)?
options: An unlawful act or omission that materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects
A dispute between two commercial airlines over landing slots
Any nuisance committed on private residential land
A minor boundary dispute between two rural agricultural tenants
10.explanation: PYA Quarries defined public nuisance as an act/omission that materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of a class of the public.

10.question: When can an individual citizen sue in public nuisance in their own name without the Attorney-General (Tate & Lyle v GLC 1983)?
options: When they have obtained written approval from the Lord Mayor
When they can show they suffered 'special damage' (particular damage over and above that suffered by the rest of the public)
Whenever they reside within 500 meters of the public highway
Whenever the nuisance involves an obstruction of a public footpath
10.explanation: An individual can sue in public nuisance only if they suffer 'special damage'—direct and substantial damage greater than that suffered by the general public.

10.question: What are the four essential elements of the rule in Rylands v Fletcher (1868)?
options: Intentional damage to chattels; malice; physical trespass; and financial fraud
Breach of contract; pure economic loss; negligence; and novus actus interveniens
Defamation; publication to third parties; injury to trade; and conspiracy
Bringing onto land and keeping something likely to do mischief if it escapes; a non-natural use of land; an escape; and resulting foreseeable damage
10.explanation: Rylands v Fletcher requires: (1) bringing onto land/accumulating something likely to do mischief; (2) non-natural use of land; (3) escape; (4) foreseeable damage.

10.question: In Transco plc v Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council (2003), how did the House of Lords define 'non-natural use' and the scope of Rylands v Fletcher?
options: An extraordinary and unusual use of land creating an exceptionally high risk of danger, not ordinary domestic piped water
Building residential high-rise flats in an urban area
Any use of land that produces industrial or commercial profits
Constructing public municipal highways and drainage systems
10.explanation: In Transco, the House of Lords affirmed Rylands is a strict liability sub-species of nuisance: non-natural use means extraordinary/unusual risk; domestic water is natural.

10.question: In Read v J Lyons & Co Ltd (1947), why did the Rylands v Fletcher claim fail when an explosion injured an inspector inside a munitions factory?
options: Because the inspector was an undischarged bankrupt
Because munitions factories enjoy royal prerogative immunity
Because explosives are natural uses of land during wartime
Because there was no 'escape'; escape requires the dangerous thing to move from a place under D's control to a place outside D's control
10.explanation: In Read v Lyons, the explosion occurred inside the factory; Rylands v Fletcher requires an escape from the defendant's land to outside land.

10.question: In Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather plc (1994), what requirement did Lord Goff establish for liability under Rylands v Fletcher?
options: The type of damage caused by the escape must be reasonably foreseeable at the time of the accumulation
Liability is absolute regardless of whether any damage was foreseeable
The claimant must prove the defendant acted with intentional malice
The claim is barred if the chemicals seeped through porous rock
10.explanation: In Cambridge Water, Lord Goff held that foreseeability of the kind of damage caused by the escape is an essential prerequisite in Rylands v Fletcher.

10.question: What is 'Assault' as an actionable tort in English law (Collins v Wilcock 1984)?
options: An intentional act that causes another person to reasonably apprehend the immediate infliction of unlawful force upon them
The unlawful detention of a person without legal justification
The actual intentional and direct application of physical force to another
A verbal argument between two commercial business rivals
10.explanation: Assault is an intentional act that directly causes the claimant to reasonably apprehend immediate unlawful physical violence.

10.question: In Tuberville v Savage (1669), why did the defendant's words, 'If it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you', negate assault?
options: Because the weapon was sheathed in a leather scabbard
Because his words explicitly showed he had no intention to strike the claimant at that present moment
Because insulting words are actionable only in slander
Because assize judges enjoyed physical immunity from violence
10.explanation: In Tuberville v Savage, words accompanying an act can negate assault by explaining away any threatening appearance of immediate violence.

10.question: In R v Ireland; R v Burstow (1997), can silent telephone calls constitute an assault in law?
options: Yes, but only if the calls were made between midnight and 6:00 am
No, an assault strictly requires physical gestures with weapons
No, phone calls are governed exclusively by telecommunications statutes
Yes, silent phone calls causing fear of immediate violence can amount to an assault
10.explanation: In R v Ireland, silent telephone calls were held capable of constituting assault where they induce a fear of imminent, immediate unlawful violence.

10.question: What is 'Battery' as an intentional tort (Collins v Wilcock 1984)?
options: Accidentally bumping into someone in a crowded shopping street
The actual intentional and direct application of unlawful physical force to the person of another without consent
Detaining a suspect in a police vehicle under a lawful arrest warrant
Making verbal threats of future violence in a private letter
10.explanation: Battery is the intentional direct application of unlawful force to another person without consent (Collins v Wilcock).

10.question: In Cole v Turner (1704) and Collins v Wilcock (1984), how does the law treat the ordinary physical jostling of everyday life?
options: It is punishable by summary arrest without a warrant
It constitutes common assault under s.39 CJA 1988
It is not battery; there is an implied consent or general social exception for the ordinary physical contacts of everyday life
It is actionable per se and entitles the victim to £500 statutory damages
10.explanation: In Collins v Wilcock, Goff LJ noted that the exigencies of everyday life create an exception: ordinary jostling on a bus or pavement is not battery.

10.question: What are the essential elements of the tort of 'False Imprisonment' (Bird v Jones 1845)?
options: Detaining a criminal suspect under an official court remand order
Restricting a person's movement in one specific direction while leaving other exits open
The total and intentional restraint of the claimant's liberty without lawful justification, without any reasonable means of escape
Failing to answer a telephone call from a family relative
10.explanation: In Bird v Jones, false imprisonment requires complete, total restriction of liberty; blocking one direction while other ways were open is not false imprisonment.

10.question: In Meering v Grahame-White Aviation Co Ltd (1919), can a person be falsely imprisoned without being aware of it at the time?
options: Yes, but only if the detention lasted for longer than 24 hours
Yes, a person can be falsely imprisoned while asleep, unconscious, intoxicated, or unaware of the restraint
No, unless the victim suffered physical trauma during the detention
No, knowledge of the detention is an absolute prerequisite to establishing the tort
10.explanation: In Meering, Atkin LJ held that a person can be falsely imprisoned without knowing of it at the time (e.g. while asleep, drunk, or mad).

10.question: What is the tort under the rule in Wilkinson v Downton (1897)?
options: Negligent maintenance of railway station lighting
Fraudulent conversion of corporate share certificates
Intentionally and without justification doing an act calculated to cause physical harm or psychiatric illness to the claimant, which in fact produces such harm
Trespass to land accompanied by foul language
10.explanation: Wilkinson v Downton established liability for intentionally causing physical harm or psychiatric injury through false statements (practical joke about husband's legs broken).

10.question: What is 'Vicarious Liability' in English tort law?
options: A form of strict secondary liability where an employer is held legally responsible for the torts committed by an employee in the course of employment
Liability imposed on a landlord for the personal debts of a tenant
Liability imposed on doctors for defective surgical instruments
A criminal sanction imposed on trade unions for calling unlawful strikes
10.explanation: Vicarious liability holds an employer strictly liable for torts committed by an employee in the course of their employment.

10.question: What test did the Court of Appeal establish in Ready Mixed Concrete (South East) Ltd v Minister of Pensions (1968) to identify an employee (contract of service)?
options: The 'Multiple/Economic Reality' test: remuneration in exchange for personal service; degree of control by master; and terms consistent with a contract of service
The organizational integration test looking solely at trade union membership
The statutory test under the Companies Act 2006
The pure control test looking solely at whether the master supervises every hour of work
10.explanation: Ready Mixed Concrete established the modern multi-factorial/economic reality test: wage for personal service, control, and other provisions consistent with employment.

10.question: In Catholic Child Welfare Society v Various Claimants (2012), how did the Supreme Court expand vicarious liability beyond traditional employment?
options: By abolishing the distinction between employees and independent contractors
By making religious orders strictly liable for international disputes
By establishing the 'relationship akin to employment' test, where the relationship has similar characteristics to employment
By making charities liable for all crimes in their geographic county
10.explanation: In Catholic Child Welfare Society (The Christian Brothers), Lord Phillips established that vicarious liability applies to relationships 'akin to employment'.

10.question: Under the 'Salmond Test', when is a tort committed by an employee 'in the course of employment'?
options: Only if the employer expressly ordered the employee to commit the exact tort in writing
Whenever an employee is wearing the corporate uniform
If it is either an act authorized by the employer, or an unauthorized mode of doing some act that was authorized
Whenever an employee commits any tort between 9:00 am and 5:00 pm
10.explanation: The Salmond test: an employer is liable for authorized acts, or unauthorized modes of doing authorized acts (e.g. Century Insurance v Northern Ireland RTB).

10.question: In Lister v Hesley Hall Ltd (2001), what modern test did the House of Lords establish for vicarious liability for intentional wrongful acts/crimes?
options: The strict authorization test requiring board approval
The course of business test looking only at accounting profits
The criminal conviction test requiring a crown court trial
The 'Close Connection' test: whether the tort was so closely connected with the employee's employment that it would be fair and just to hold the employer vicariously liable
10.explanation: Lister v Hesley Hall established the 'close connection' test: is the tort so closely connected with employment that it is fair and just to hold the employer liable?

10.question: In Joel v Morison (1834), how did Parke B describe an employee acting outside the course of employment?
options: Violating commercial transport regulations
Engaging in an unlawful industrial picket
Committing high treason against the Crown
Going on a 'frolic of his own', without being at all on his master's business
10.explanation: In Joel v Morison, Parke B famously stated that if a master's servant is going on a 'frolic of his own', the master is not liable.

10.question: In Century Insurance Co Ltd v Northern Ireland Road Transport Board (1942), why was the employer liable when a petrol tanker driver lit a cigarette while unloading fuel, causing an explosion?
options: Because the employer had purchased catastrophic explosion insurance
Because he was performing an authorized task (unloading petrol) in an unauthorized and negligent mode
Because smoking was permitted under his trade union agreement
Because petrol stations are subject to strict statutory liability under Rylands v Fletcher
10.explanation: In Century Insurance, the driver was doing an authorized act (delivering petrol) in an unauthorized/negligent manner, so the employer was vicariously liable.

10.question: What is the primary objective of an award of compensatory damages in the law of tort (Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co 1880)?
options: To impose a moral penance on the tortfeasor
To put the injured party in the same position as they would have been in if the tort had not been committed, so far as money can do so (restitutio in integrum)
To redistribute corporate wealth to individual consumers
To punish the defendant and enrich the state treasury
10.explanation: Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co: compensatory damages in tort aim to put the claimant in the position they would have been in had the tort not occurred.

10.question: What is the difference between 'Special Damages' and 'General Damages' in a tort claim?
options: Special damages cover quantifiable past financial losses up to trial (e.g. lost wages, medical bills); General damages cover non-pecuniary losses (pain, suffering) and future financial loss
Special damages are awarded by a jury; general damages are set by statute
Special damages are capped at £5,000; general damages are unlimited
Special damages are awarded only in defamation; general damages apply in all other torts
10.explanation: Special damages represent precise, itemized financial losses incurred up to the date of trial; general damages cover pain, suffering, loss of amenity, and future losses.

10.question: What are 'Aggravated Damages' in tort?
options: Damages that double the statutory limitation period
Criminal fines paid to the Crown Prosecution Service
Damages awarded to compensate the claimant for additional distress or injury to feelings caused by the defendant's bad faith, spite, or malicious conduct
Damages designed to punish the defendant for breach of statutory duty
10.explanation: Aggravated damages are compensatory in nature, compensating for increased mental distress caused by the manner/malice of D's conduct (Rookes v Barnard).

10.question: Under Rookes v Barnard (1964), when are 'Exemplary (Punitive) Damages' permitted in English tort law?
options: In all medical negligence claims involving NHS trusts
Oppressive, arbitrary, or unconstitutional conduct by servants of the government; conduct calculated by D to make a profit exceeding potential compensation; or where authorized by statute
In any case where the claimant is offended by the defendant's conduct
Whenever a contract is breached with pre-meditated intention
10.explanation: Under Rookes v Barnard, exemplary (punitive) damages are strictly limited to government oppression, profit-seeking wrongdoing, or express statutory authority.

10.question: What is a 'Prohibitory Injunction' in tort law?
options: An order commanding the police to arrest an undischarged debtor
An order compelling the defendant to pay money into the High Court
An equitable order from the court restraining the defendant from committing, continuing, or repeating a tortious act (e.g. continuing a nuisance)
An order barring the claimant from consulting a solicitor
10.explanation: A prohibitory injunction is an equitable court order forbidding the defendant from commencing or continuing a wrongful act (e.g. continuing a nuisance).

10.question: What is a 'Mandatory Injunction'?
options: A decree dissolving an incorporated business partnership
A warrant issued by the Crown Court for jury selection
An equitable court order requiring the defendant to take positive steps to undo a wrongful state of affairs (e.g. demolishing a building erected in breach of rights)
A notice demanding payment of local business rates
10.explanation: A mandatory injunction compels the defendant to take positive action to restore the status quo or rectify the consequences of a tortious act.

10.question: What principles govern the award of interim (interlocutory) injunctions as established in American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd (1975)?
options: A financial bond of £1,000,000 deposited in the High Court
Serious question to be tried; balance of convenience; and whether damages would be an adequate remedy for either party
Mandatory referral to the Court of Appeal before granting relief
Proof beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant acted maliciously
10.explanation: American Cyanamid guidelines: (1) is there a serious question to be tried? (2) would damages be adequate? (3) where does the balance of convenience lie?

10.question: Under the rule in Shelfer v City of London Electric Lighting Co (1895), when may a court award damages in lieu of an injunction for nuisance?
options: Whenever the nuisance has lasted for less than six calendar months
Whenever the claimant is willing to accept a commercial voucher
Injury to C's rights is small; capable of being estimated in money; can be adequately compensated by a small money payment; and granting an injunction would be oppressive to D
Whenever the defendant is a registered public utility company
10.explanation: Shelfer sets out the 4 criteria where damages in lieu of an injunction may be granted: small injury, money quantifiable, small payment adequate, and injunction oppressive.

10.question: How did the Supreme Court in Coventry v Lawrence (2014) modify the application of the Shelfer rule on injunctions in nuisance?
options: Courts should exercise a more flexible discretion when deciding whether to award damages instead of an injunction, considering the public interest
The Shelfer rule was completely abolished and replaced by statutory arbitration
Damages can only be awarded if both parties agree in writing
Injunctions are now mandatory in all nuisance cases without exception
10.explanation: In Coventry v Lawrence, the Supreme Court held that the Shelfer criteria should not be applied rigidly; courts have broader, flexible discretion considering public interest.

10.question: What is the equitable remedy of 'Specific Performance' in contract law?
options: A warrant authorizing the bailiff to seize commercial goods
A financial penalty imposed on a contractor who completes a project late
An order terminating the contract and forfeiting all deposit funds
A court order compelling a party to perform their positive contractual obligations (used when damages are inadequate, e.g. contracts for unique land or rare chattels)
10.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable decree ordering a party to carry out their positive contractual promise; granted where damages are inadequate (e.g. land, unique goods).
